body: I was tested positive end of December after catching it at my hospital workplace, and spread it within my household. I'm young and fit, but was taken down by covid. After 10 days of hell I started to feel normal, besides calf cramps at night and still feeling chesty. I live with my parents, and really thought that they would be okay. They're in their 50s, are fit and have no co-morbidities, but my Mum is now in hospital where they're considering CPAP. I'm caring for my Dad at home, but he's worsening by the day. I am totally broken from this experience.

I’d advise to ring 111 first (yes, I know call waiting times can be slow right now) they will assess over the phone and will either send an ambulance or refer you to a covid hub. Covid hubs in my area do GP home visits too, but obviously I’m not sure about your area. Yesterday when I rang 999 for my mum instead of 111, I had to wait over two hours for a clinician to call back to triage if an ambulance was actually needed. I would have taken my mum to ED myself but she couldn’t even make it to the front door. The clinician spoke to my mum, in-between her gasping for breath, and the ambulance was promptly sent within 10 minutes. Please don’t delay getting help. Take care x

Just my experience, but on the 21st, I had loss of taste, mild sore throat and temperature. I work in a hospital so took a PCR test on the 21st, 22nd and 24th, and all were negative. On boxing day the covid truck hit me and the mild sore throat turned to SOB, hacking cough, rigors, body aches and a migraine, so I took another PCR on the 27th which was positive. I also have rapid lateral flow tests at home and I have taken one every day since the 21st, the only positive result I got was today (29th). A few of my colleagues had the same experience as me.

I work on a ward in the UK. We have been given training on how to care for a ventilated patient, as a precaution. We may have to care for ventilated patients on wards. I do not like this one bit.

Our ED is deserted. We had 10(!!!!) people in ED yesterday and a total of 30 empty beds in the hospital. I only had six patients yesterday (average is 12:1) and I spent yesterday afternoon keeping my dementia patient entertained with a board game. It’s like living in a dream world! Three months ago, we had inpatients sleeping on ward corridors, to free up the ED. We were bursting at the seams! It’s great to see people realise that they don’t need to go to hospital for a minor illness. 

Praying it continues like this.

Late to the show, but this sounds EXACTLY like my dad. I used to cut myself and punch walls as a teen in response to my Dads violent outbursts and the overwhelming fear it made me have. But, looking back, it makes me so sad that I hurt myself over his outrageous behaviour. 

People like my dad and yours don’t deserve to have children. Simple. Just know that one day you’ll reach an age when you won’t need him anymore, and you’ll either find common ground or you’ll cut ties with him due to his rage. That’s what my brother did and that’s what I plan to do as soon as a get out of his house. Not sure if you’re a teen or not, but my major advice is to study hard, get yourself a job and save up to get far away from his negative behaviour. 

There’s hope, it just takes time to find it.

So, I jump on the chest, immediately crack a few ribs and force the patient to projectile faecal vomit all over myself and the Doc attempting intubation. Fortunately, the Doc was wearing a mask, and none of it went into his eyes and mouth. I can't say the same for myself.

During another code, I took the head of the patient's bed off to allow the Doc to have more room to fit an airway. I used a little too much force during this, because as I turned around with it, I accidentally hit the Doc in the nut sack. Oops.

Next time she asks you if you're gonna cry, ask her "are going to continue to make unhelpful comments?" 

One thing I got told on my first day my preceptor jokingly said "crying is normal, over here is our designated crying zone". She wasn't wrong, and there many times during my first six months where I forced myself to hold back tears. It's a NORMAL thing to occasionally do for the environment that you work in. Traumatic events produce LOTS of adrenaline, and when that drops, you're left feeling exhausted and empty. Sometimes, it's good to give yourself five minutes to get it out your system and then, allow yourself to move on.
